questions.q: Which of the following is a primary function of the Nigerian National Assembly when exercising its legislative powers?
options: Conducting monetary policy through interest rates
Interpreting the constitution in final disputes
Making laws for the peace, order and good government of the federation
Appointing state governors
questions.explanation: The National Assembly's core role is to make laws for the peace, order and good government of the federation. Appointing state governors is done by elections, not the legislature; interpreting the constitution is the judiciary's role; monetary policy is the Central Bank's responsibility.

questions.q: A bill passed by both chambers of the National Assembly but rejected by the President can still become law if which of the following occurs?
options: Supreme Court orders it to be made law
The President signs it after a six-month waiting period
A national referendum approves the bill
Two-thirds majority of each chamber votes to pass the bill again
questions.explanation: If the President withholds assent, the National Assembly can override the veto with a two-thirds majority in each chamber. The Supreme Court cannot make a bill law; referenda are not required for ordinary bills; there is no automatic assent after six months.

questions.q: Which of these is a reason a member of the House of Representatives may lose their seat under the 1999 Constitution (as amended)?
options: Being appointed a minister in the state government
Voting against the majority view of their constituency
Becoming a citizen of another country by registration or naturalisation
Missing three consecutive sittings without a note
questions.explanation: The constitution disqualifies someone who becomes a citizen of another country by registration or naturalisation. Disagreeing with constituents or missing sittings without leave may cause political consequences but not automatic loss; state government ministerial appointments don't apply to federal representatives.

questions.q: Which office is primarily responsible for appointing federal ministers in Nigeria?
options: The Chief Justice on the advice of the National Judicial Council
The Vice-President acting alone
The National Assembly by majority vote
The President with confirmation by the Senate
questions.explanation: The President nominates ministers, who must be confirmed by the Senate. The Chief Justice and NJC deal with judicial appointments; the National Assembly does not appoint ministers directly; the Vice-President cannot appoint ministers alone.

questions.q: Which principle ensures that judges in Nigeria are independent and can decide cases without influence from the executive?
options: Removal by popular referendum after each term
Senatorial confirmation of every judgment
Security of tenure during good behaviour and financial independence
Annual reappointment by the President
questions.explanation: Judicial independence is protected by security of tenure (removal only by prescribed processes) and financial autonomy. Senatorial confirmation of judgments, annual reappointment, or removal by referendum would undermine independence and are not constitutional practices.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the doctrine of separation of powers in Nigeria?
options: Merging of legislature and judiciary to expedite laws
Complete independence so branches never interact with each other
Fusion of executive and legislature under one person
Division of government functions among legislature, executive and judiciary to prevent concentration of power
questions.explanation: Separation of powers divides functions among the three branches to check abuses. It does not mean they never interact (checks and balances require interaction), nor does it merge branches or fuse executive and legislature under one person.

questions.q: Which of the following is a constitutional method by which a person born in Nigeria can lose Nigerian citizenship?
options: Travelling abroad for more than ten years
Voluntarily acquiring the citizenship of another country
Voting for an opposition political party
Failing to pay taxes for five years
questions.explanation: The constitution allows loss of citizenship by voluntarily acquiring another nationality. Political choices, non-payment of taxes, or long stays abroad do not automatically terminate citizenship.

questions.q: Which factor most directly influences public opinion in Nigeria during election campaigns?
options: Media coverage and political messaging
The official language of neighbouring countries
Annual migration statistics
The number of public holidays in a year
questions.explanation: Media coverage and political messaging shape voters' perceptions and are primary influences on public opinion. Neighbouring countries' official languages, migration statistics, or public holiday counts have little direct effect on campaign opinions.

questions.q: Which ECOWAS mechanism was used to restore democracy after coups in member states and sometimes involved Nigeria leading regional intervention?
options: UN Security Council peacekeeping directly under ECOWAS command
ECOWAS Standby Force and diplomatic pressure (Protocol on Non-Aggression and Democracy)
African Union court issuing fines to coup leaders
World Trade Organization sanctions enforced by ECOWAS
questions.explanation: ECOWAS has protocols, diplomatic pressure and a Standby Force to respond to unconstitutional changes; Nigeria has led such interventions. The UN Security Council peacekeeping is separate; the AU Court doesn't fine coup leaders; the WTO deals with trade, not coups.

questions.q: Nigeria chaired the ECOWAS Mediation on a neighbouring crisis. Which of these is a primary purpose of ECOWAS as a regional organisation?
options: Replace national governments with a federal West African state
Enforce a single national currency for all African states
Promote economic integration, peace and security among West African states
Administer the African Union's judicial system
questions.explanation: ECOWAS aims to promote economic integration and maintain peace and security in West Africa. It does not enforce a single continent-wide currency, replace national governments with a federal state, or administer the AU's courts.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes a federal system like Nigeria from a unitary system?
options: The central government delegates authority informally without constitutional guarantee
Constitutional division of powers between central and regional governments
All laws originate exclusively from traditional rulers
Regions are free to secede at will without constitutional process
questions.explanation: Federal systems have constitutionally guaranteed divisions of power between central and regional units. Laws do not originate solely from traditional rulers; regions cannot secede at will; informal delegation without constitutional protection describes a unitary or decentralised system, not true federalism.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why political parties in Nigeria adopt manifestos during campaigns?
options: To set judicial guidelines for interpreting party laws
To appoint party officials at local government level
To present policy proposals and attract voters by outlining party objectives
To register the party with the Independent National Electoral Commission
questions.explanation: Party manifestos are documents that outline policies and programmes to persuade voters; they are not administrative registration instruments (that is INEC's role) nor internal appointment or judicial guideline documents.

questions.q: A pressure group in Nigeria wants to influence oil policy without seeking elective office. Which method is most characteristic of pressure group activity?
options: Conducting judicial review to change laws
Amending the Constitution through a referendum
Fielding candidates in gubernatorial elections
Lobbying members of the National Assembly and organizing public campaigns
questions.explanation: Pressure groups typically lobby legislators and mobilize public opinion; they do not run for office (that's what parties do), cannot unilaterally amend the constitution (requires specific constitutional procedures), and cannot directly perform judicial review—courts do that.

questions.q: Which factor most weakens political party institutionalization in Nigeria?
options: Strong grassroots party structures across all wards
Frequent party defections by politicians for short-term advantage
Clear ideological differences maintained over time
Transparent internal party elections conducted regularly
questions.explanation: Frequent defections undermine stable party identity and organization. Strong grassroots structures, clear consistent ideology, and transparent internal elections strengthen institutionalization, not weaken it.

questions.q: Which constitutional principle requires that government power be shared among separate institutions in Nigeria?
options: Supremacy of the legislature
Separation of powers
Judicial activism
Popular sovereignty
questions.explanation: Separation of powers divides functions among legislature, executive and judiciary. Supremacy of the legislature is not a constitutional principle in Nigeria; judicial activism is a behaviour of courts, and popular sovereignty refers to authority from the people, not institutional separation.

questions.q: Under the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria (as amended), which body has the power to amend most sections of the Constitution?
options: The Supreme Court by declaration
The Independent National Electoral Commission
National Assembly with approval by two-thirds of state Houses of Assembly where required
The President acting alone by executive order
questions.explanation: Constitutional amendment generally requires action by the National Assembly and, for certain provisions, approval by two-thirds of state Houses of Assembly. The President cannot unilaterally amend the Constitution; the Supreme Court interprets law but does not amend it; INEC administers elections.

questions.q: Which of the following is a feature of a written constitution as in Nigeria?
options: A single formal document that sets out fundamental laws and structures of government
A secret set of rules available only to government officials
A constantly changing list of conventions decided by Parliament on the day
A set of informal traditions with no legal force
questions.explanation: A written constitution is a formal, codified document accessible to the public that outlines government structure and rights. Informal traditions and conventions without legal force describe unwritten constitutions; secrecy is not a feature of written constitutions.

questions.q: Which of these powers is typically exercised by state governments under Nigerian federalism?
options: Printing Naira notes and coins
Management of primary and secondary education within the state
Maintenance of national currency and foreign policy
Issuing passports and regulating international trade
questions.explanation: States in Nigeria are responsible for primary and secondary education. Currency, foreign policy, passports, international trade regulation, and printing currency are federal responsibilities.

questions.q: Which feature helps maintain cooperation between the federal and state governments in Nigeria?
options: Exclusive state control of national defence forces
Revenue allocation formulas and federal transfers to states
State power to sign international treaties independently
Complete fiscal autonomy of each local government without federal oversight
questions.explanation: Revenue allocation formulas and federal transfers are central to fiscal relations and cooperation. Local governments do not have complete fiscal autonomy, national defence is federal, and states cannot independently sign treaties—that is a federal power.

questions.q: Which concept best describes a government's right to rule accepted by the people in Nigeria?
options: Authority without consent
Coercion
Legitimacy
Force
questions.explanation: Legitimacy is acceptance by the governed that the government has a right to rule. Coercion and force can compel obedience but do not imply rightful acceptance; 'authority without consent' contradicts the idea of legitimacy.

questions.q: If the Federal Government of Nigeria decides a matter and no other authority can override that decision within the country, this describes which political concept?
options: Popular consensus
Sovereignty
Delegated authority
Legitimacy
questions.explanation: Sovereignty refers to supreme legal authority within a territory, meaning no internal authority can override it. Legitimacy concerns acceptance, delegated authority is power given by another body, and popular consensus is agreement among people, not the sole legal supremacy implied by sovereignty.

questions.q: Under the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, which of the following rights is explicitly protected as a fundamental right?
options: Right to inherit property from the state
Right to unlimited bail in all cases
Right to run for office without meeting age requirements
Freedom of assembly and association
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution lists freedom of assembly and association among Fundamental Rights (Chapter IV). The other options are not guaranteed: inheritance from the state is not a fundamental right, bail can be denied in certain serious cases, and age qualifications for office are constitutionally required.

questions.q: Which amendment/ change in Nigeria's constitutional history is most associated with the introduction of state governors elected by universal adult suffrage?
options: The 1960 Independence Constitution
The 1963 Republican Constitution
The 1979 Constitution establishing the Second Republic
The 1999 Constitution after military rule
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution created a presidential system with elected state governors chosen by universal adult suffrage. The 1960 Independence Constitution and 1963 Republican Constitution retained parliamentary features with different regional arrangements, while the 1999 Constitution restored elected governors after military rule but the key institutional shift to elected governors began in 1979.

questions.q: Which of these was a common justification given by military regimes in Nigeria for suspending the constitution and dissolving democratic institutions?
options: To immediately hand over power to traditional rulers
To replace the naira with a military currency
To restore law, order and eliminate corruption seen as threatening national unity
To introduce a multi‑party parliamentary system
questions.explanation: Military regimes often claimed they intervened to restore order and tackle corruption and threats to unity. They did not justify coups by promising rule by traditional rulers, changing currency to a special military issue, or instituting parliamentary systems — those were not standard military claims.

questions.q: During military rule in Nigeria, the instrument used by military heads to make laws and govern without the National Assembly was usually called what?
options: Federal Edict
Civil Code
Proclamation of Parliament
Decree
questions.explanation: Military governments in Nigeria governed by Decrees which had the force of law without legislative approval. 'Proclamation of Parliament' and 'Civil Code' are incorrect terms, and 'Edict' is usually the term for state military law but the federal instrument used by heads of state was called a Decree.

questions.q: Which Nigerian military leader is associated with the transition programme that produced the Third Republic aborted in the early 1990s and annulment of June 12, 1993 election?
options: General Yakubu Gowon
General Murtala Mohammed
General Ibrahim Babangida
General Sani Abacha
questions.explanation: General Ibrahim Babangida presided over the transition that led to the annulled June 12, 1993 presidential election. Gowon, Murtala and Abacha were military leaders at other times; Abacha later seized power after the transition collapsed but was not responsible for the 1993 annulment.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes Nigeria’s role in ECOWAS during the 1990s and 2000s?
options: Leading regional peacekeeping and mediation efforts in West Africa
Adopting a policy of strict non‑intervention in member states' crises
Becoming a financial vassal of European Union policies
Withdrawing from ECOWAS institutions to focus on domestic issues
questions.explanation: Nigeria played a leading role in ECOWAS peacekeeping and mediation, intervening in conflicts in Liberia and Sierra Leone. It did not adopt strict non‑intervention, withdraw from ECOWAS, nor become a financial vassal of EU policies; rather it used regional mechanisms for stability.

questions.q: Which policy objective explains why Nigeria often seeks leadership positions in African and multilateral organisations?
options: To relocate its capital to another African country
To project influence and protect national economic and security interests regionally
To renounce all bilateral relations outside Africa
To limit Nigerian trade to only ECOWAS members
questions.explanation: Nigeria seeks leadership in regional and international organisations to advance its influence and safeguard economic and security interests. The wrong options are unrealistic and contrary to Nigeria's active international engagement.

questions.topic: Separation of powers and checks and balances
questions.q: If the President of Nigeria vetoes a bill passed by the National Assembly, what constitutional mechanism allows the National Assembly to still make that bill law?
options: Override of the veto by a two‑thirds majority in both chambers
A Supreme Court declaration without legislative action
A written consent from the state governors
A public referendum held automatically
questions.explanation: The Constitution allows the National Assembly to override a presidential veto with a two‑thirds majority in both the Senate and House of Representatives. Judicial declaration, referendum, or state governors' consent do not override a federal presidential veto.

questions.topic: Separation of powers and checks and balances
questions.q: Which of the following is a clear example of judicial review as a check on the legislative branch in Nigeria?
options: The Supreme Court declaring an Act of the National Assembly unconstitutional
The National Assembly impeaching a judge
State governors passing local ordinances
The President appointing new legislators
questions.explanation: Judicial review occurs when the judiciary (e.g., the Supreme Court) declares an Act of the National Assembly unconstitutional, thereby checking legislative power. Impeaching a judge is a legislative check on the judiciary, the President cannot appoint legislators, and state ordinances are not judicial review.

questions.q: Which electoral system is most likely to produce a single-party majority in the Nigerian House of Representatives even if that party gets less than 50% of the national vote?
options: Mixed-member proportional representation
Single transferable vote in multimember districts
First-past-the-post (single-member plurality)
Proportional representation with party lists
questions.explanation: First-past-the-post (single-member plurality) awards each constituency to the candidate with the most votes, so a party can win many seats without a majority of the national vote. Proportional representation would allocate seats roughly by vote share; single transferable vote and mixed-member proportional aim to reduce disparities between votes and seats.

questions.q: Which reform would most directly reduce the number of spoilt ballots in a Nigerian presidential election?
options: Changing to proportional representation for presidential contests
Raising the minimum voting age to 21
Introducing compulsory voting with heavy fines
Simplifying ballot design and providing clear voting instructions at polling units
questions.explanation: Spoilt ballots are usually caused by voter confusion or mistakes; clearer ballot design and instructions directly address this. Raising voting age does not target ballot spoiling, compulsory voting may increase spoilt ballots, and proportional representation is irrelevant for a single-winner presidential election.

questions.q: Which practice best describes 'zoning' as used by Nigerian political parties?
options: Formally mandating that only one party may contest certain zones
Using primary elections open only to party leaders
Allocating parliamentary seats to parties based strictly on vote share
Informally rotating key elective offices among geopolitical zones to balance representation
questions.explanation: Zoning is an informal arrangement to rotate offices among regions to promote inclusiveness. It is not a formal legal restriction, nor a seat-allocation formula based on votes, and it is unrelated to who may participate in primaries.

questions.q: Under the 1999 Constitution, which body has the power to confirm the appointment of a federal minister in Nigeria?
options: The National Judicial Council
The House of Representatives
The Senate
The Federal Executive Council (cabinet)
questions.explanation: The Constitution requires Senate confirmation for certain federal appointments; ministers are appointed by the President but must be presented to the National Assembly, with the Senate playing the primary confirmation role. The House of Representatives does not confirm ministers, the NJC handles judicial appointments, and the Federal Executive Council is the cabinet itself, not a confirming body.

questions.q: Which action by the judiciary would be an example of judicial review in Nigeria?
options: A High Court sentencing a defendant in a criminal trial
The Chief Justice appointing an acting judge temporarily
Declaring a law passed by the National Assembly inconsistent with the Constitution and thus invalid
The Supreme Court issuing writs to enforce police orders
questions.explanation: Judicial review is the courts' power to assess whether legislation conflicts with the Constitution and to invalidate it. Issuing writs or sentencing defendants are judicial functions but not review of constitutionality; the Chief Justice appointing acting judges is administrative, not judicial review.

questions.q: Which of these most directly measures public opinion in Nigeria on a policy issue?
options: A scientifically sampled opinion poll with clear questions and reported margins of error
A newspaper editorial arguing a position
A statement by a prominent traditional ruler
A petition signed by a few thousand people
questions.explanation: A properly conducted scientific poll is designed to represent the population's views and includes methodology and margin of error. Editorials, petitions, and elite statements reflect particular voices or advocacy but do not directly measure the broader public opinion.

questions.q: Which right is typically associated with active citizenship in a democracy like Nigeria?
options: Claiming exemptions from taxation without due process
Denial of access to public schools for dissenting citizens
Participating in peaceful demonstrations to express views on public policy
Using violence to overthrow an elected government
questions.explanation: Active citizenship includes exercising civil rights such as peaceful assembly to influence public policy. The wrong options describe illegal or undemocratic actions: tax exemption without process, violent overthrow, and denial of services are not acceptable forms of civic engagement.

questions.q: Which UN organ is primarily responsible for maintaining international peace and security and can authorise peacekeeping operations that Nigeria participates in?
options: The General Assembly
The Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC)
The International Court of Justice
The Security Council
questions.explanation: The UN Security Council is mandated to maintain international peace and security and authorises peacekeeping missions. The General Assembly discusses broad issues but cannot authorise binding peace operations; the ICJ settles legal disputes between states; ECOSOC handles economic and social matters.

questions.q: Which ECOWAS mechanism was used to respond quickly to the 2015 political crisis in The Gambia and involved deployment of troops from member states including Nigeria?
options: The ECOWAS Court of Justice issuing an immediate ruling
A special session of the African Union Peace and Security Council without ECOWAS involvement
A trade sanction enforced by the ECOWAS Commission
A standby force for crisis response authorised by ECOWAS heads of state
questions.explanation: ECOWAS authorised a standby force to intervene and restore constitutional order in The Gambia; this military deployment was coordinated by member states. The ECOWAS Court cannot deploy troops; trade sanctions are not the rapid military response used; while the AU may have been consulted, the rapid troop deployment was an ECOWAS action.

questions.q: Which ECOWAS organ has the final authority to approve the use of collective military force by the Community (for example, to restore constitutional order in a member state)?
options: Community Court of Justice
ECOWAS Parliament
Authority of Heads of State and Government
Council of Ministers
questions.explanation: The Authority of Heads of State and Government is ECOWAS's highest decision-making body and has the power to give final approval for collective military action. The Council of Ministers prepares and implements policies but does not have final authority on the use of force. The ECOWAS Parliament is mainly consultative/legislative and cannot authorise military intervention, while the Community Court of Justice settles legal disputes rather than approving force.
